title: Closing market recap : Nov 6, 2026
summary: A tech-led rebound lifted the market at the close, powered by upbeat chip and travel earnings. Next, investors will watch Berkshire’s results and the final readings on today’s economic data to see if gains can spread beyond technology.

sections.heading: Market overview
sections.text: Stocks finished higher at the close on Friday, with the S&P 500 up slightly and the Nasdaq-focused QQQ gaining about 1.5%. Big technology names helped offset weakness in more defensive areas, hinting at a cautious shift back toward growth stocks.

sections.heading: Sector and industry performance
sections.text: Technology was the clear winner, helped by strong semiconductor and hardware gains. Financials, consumer staples, and real estate generally fell, showing that more traditional, steady sectors lost favor for the day.

sections.heading: Stock movers and news
sections.text: Advanced Micro Devices jumped around 11% after reporting better-than-expected results earlier this week and strong data center growth. Airbnb climbed about 12% as investors continued to reward its solid quarterly demand and raised outlook.

sections.heading: Stock movers and news
sections.text: AppLovin rose roughly 10% as its post-earnings rally extended, despite a reminder about a pending shareholder lawsuit deadline. Power producer Vistra gained about 10% after its recent earnings call, while Axon slid more than 18% without a clear news driver in this feed.

sections.heading: Reported earnings
sections.text: Moderna surprised with a profit instead of the loss analysts expected, and Enbridge beat profit and revenue forecasts. Hawaiian Electric also reported stronger-than-expected results, which may help investors reassess earlier concerns around the company.

sections.heading: Upcoming earnings
sections.text: Several smaller companies were set to report after the close, but their numbers were not yet available. Tomorrow, Berkshire Hathaway’s results could give a broad snapshot of the economy through its insurance, industrial, and energy businesses.

sections.heading: Economic events
sections.text: Today’s monthly jobs report and a consumer sentiment survey were scheduled this morning, but the results were not included here. Once known, they could quickly change expectations for inflation and interest rates, especially for banks, housing, and high-growth tech names.

sections.heading: What to watch next
sections.text: A tech-led rebound lifted the market at the close, powered by upbeat chip and travel earnings. Next, investors will watch Berkshire’s results and the final readings on today’s economic data to see if gains can spread beyond technology.

title: October 26, 2026 earnings preview: AI design demand, property income and insurance margins
summary: Welltower, Cadence, Nucor and five financial and property companies are due to report after close. Watch outlooks, underlying growth and cash generation rather than headline profit alone.

sections.heading: 1) When the reports are due
sections.text: Welltower, Nucor, Public Storage, Hartford, Cincinnati Financial, Principal and Brown & Brown have announced third-quarter results for October 26 after close. Cadence has confirmed its October 26 financial-results webcast after close; its release is expected in that window. Several management calls follow on October 27, so the initial release and the fuller explanation can arrive on different days.

sections.heading: 2) Welltower: can occupancy gains keep improving margins?
sections.text: Welltower owns healthcare real estate, including senior housing. In its July 27 second-quarter report, comparable senior-housing revenue grew 9.2%, supported by more occupied rooms and higher revenue per occupied room. Tonight’s test is whether that demand continues to cover staffing and other operating costs. Investors should focus on property income and normalized funds from operations, an adjusted real-estate earnings measure, alongside cash needs for new investments.

sections.heading: 3) Cadence: a higher growth bar meets AI spending
sections.text: Cadence sells software and systems used to design chips and electronic products. Its July 27 results raised the full-year revenue-growth outlook to 19%, with an adjusted operating-margin midpoint of 44.25%. Strong customer orders support future revenue, but investors need to see how quickly those orders turn into sales and cash. Watch guidance, spending and margins together; a higher sales forecast is less valuable if costs rise faster.

sections.heading: 4) Nucor: look through temporary benefits
sections.text: Nucor makes steel and steel products. On September 17 it guided to third-quarter GAAP profit of $5.55–$5.65 per share for the quarter ending October 3. EPS means profit per share; this is company guidance, not an analyst estimate or reported result. The prior quarter benefited from $130 million of raw-material cost refunds that management did not expect to repeat. Watch steel selling prices, shipments and underlying production margins to judge the strength of demand.

sections.heading: 5) Public Storage: rental growth must beat cost growth
sections.text: Public Storage rents self-storage space. In its July 29 results it raised its full-year Core funds-from-operations guidance to $16.75–$17.05 per share, while still projecting a decline in comparable-property operating income. Core funds from operations is an adjusted real-estate earnings measure, not GAAP profit. Watch occupancy, new-customer rents and property expenses: higher company-wide earnings can coexist with pressure at existing locations.

sections.heading: 6) Hartford and Cincinnati: claims discipline matters more than portfolio gains
sections.text: Hartford sells property, casualty and employee-benefit insurance; Cincinnati Financial combines insurance underwriting with a substantial investment portfolio. Their reports should show whether premium increases are covering claims inflation and catastrophe losses. Cincinnati’s second-quarter combined ratio was 100.8%, indicating claims and underwriting expenses exceeded the premiums earned. The ratio is a useful way to separate the economics of writing policies from swings in investment values.

sections.heading: 7) A recent insurance peer sets a useful comparison
sections.text: Travelers reported third-quarter results on October 16, including a combined ratio of 86.8%. A ratio below 100% indicates an underwriting profit before investment income. Its result benefited from favorable revisions to earlier claims estimates, so investors should also examine performance excluding those revisions and catastrophe losses. Travelers offers current sector context for Hartford and Cincinnati, but different policy mixes and storm exposure can produce very different results.

sections.heading: 8) Brown & Brown: acquisition growth needs an underlying check
sections.text: Brown & Brown earns insurance-brokerage commissions and fees. Its July 27 second-quarter report showed revenue up 30.4%, but organic revenue, which strips out acquisitions and other adjustments, down 0.7%. Tonight, watch client retention, underlying revenue and the costs of integrating acquisitions. Large reported growth is more valuable when the existing business is improving and extra debt and integration spending are manageable.

sections.heading: 9) Principal: distinguish market gains from new customer money
sections.text: Principal runs retirement, asset-management and insurance businesses. Its July 27 report showed $808 billion in assets under management. That asset total affects fee income, but can rise simply because markets rise. Watch net customer flows, retirement contributions and operating margins to see whether the business is attracting new money. Market weakness, withdrawals and insurance claims remain important risks.

sections.heading: 10) How to read the releases
sections.text: Start with changes to management’s outlook, then check whether operating performance and cash support them. Compare GAAP profit with clearly labeled adjusted measures; acquisition effects, investment gains and temporary refunds can make a headline look stronger than the underlying business. These are previews of upcoming reports, not released third-quarter results or predictions of the next stock move. The app’s earnings tools offer another way to explore the companies without assuming a favorable outcome.

sections.heading: 1) The reporting lineup and expectations

sections.text:
Visa’s fiscal fourth-quarter and full-year report is confirmed for after close on October 27. The payments network earns fees as money moves through its systems. Watch payment volumes, cross-border spending and the revenue outlook for its new fiscal year.

On October 15, Visa announced an initial commercial rollout of stablecoin-enabled funding through Inyo Global. Stablecoins are digital tokens designed to track a currency’s value. The rollout gives eligible businesses another way to fund international payments. Adoption and revenue contribution are the next tests; deployment alone does not establish a large earnings benefit.
sections.heading: 2) Visa: payment growth and new revenue streams

sections.text:
Seagate’s fiscal first-quarter 2027 report is confirmed for after close on October 27. Its high-capacity hard drives serve cloud and enterprise customers. Watch whether demand supports pricing, manufacturing efficiency and cash generation, alongside the next-quarter forecast.

Memory and storage supplier Micron reported record fiscal fourth-quarter results on September 30 and cited AI demand. That provides supportive industry context, although memory chips and hard drives have different economics. Seagate still needs to show its own customer demand and margins can sustain growth.
sections.heading: 3) Seagate: storage demand must support margins

sections.text:
Robinhood’s third-quarter release is confirmed for after close on October 27. Its September 28 update covered September 1–24, including about $267 billion in equity trading, 234 million options contracts and 4.4 billion event contracts. Those were preliminary figures for part of the month.

Full September data are due with the earnings release. Watch revenue earned from that activity, customer deposits and operating costs. More trading does not translate dollar for dollar into company revenue, and activity can reverse when markets become quieter.
sections.heading: 4) Robinhood: turn trading activity into revenue

sections.text:
NXP’s third-quarter release is confirmed for after close on October 27. On October 26, it announced a strategic partnership to supply microcontrollers, chips that control vehicle functions, for Volkswagen’s future vehicle architecture. The first vehicle using that architecture is planned for 2027.

This is a future growth opportunity. Watch the current automotive and industrial outlook, customer inventory and the timing of revenue from new designs. Relevant peer Texas Instruments reported on October 21 that third-quarter revenue rose 28%, with growth across industrial, automotive and data-center markets. That recovery provides context for NXP’s own forecast.
sections.heading: 5) NXP: a new design win meets the demand outlook

sections.text:
Teradyne has confirmed its third-quarter release for after close on October 27, with its earnings call on October 28. It sells equipment that tests chips and electronics, as well as robotics systems. Watch demand for chip testing, delivery schedules and the outlook for profitability.

Texas Instruments’ October 21 results showed broader chip-market growth, but a chip supplier’s sales are not the same as orders for test equipment. The key question for Teradyne is whether customers’ manufacturing plans support sustained equipment purchases. Large orders can shift between quarters.
sections.heading: 6) Teradyne: orders will shape the next quarter

sections.text:
WM has confirmed third-quarter results after close on October 27 and its earnings call on October 28. The waste-services company’s key tests are pricing, collection and disposal volumes, labor and fuel costs, and cash left after investment spending.

Waste Connections reported third-quarter results on October 21, raised its full-year outlook and recorded an adjusted EBITDA margin of 34%, a profit measure before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. sections.heading: 7) WM: pricing must cover operating costs

sections.text:
ONEOK has confirmed third-quarter results after close on October 27 and its earnings call on October 28. Its energy transport and processing network makes the volume of products moving through its assets a key operating measure.

Watch operating cash flow, project spending and debt alongside revenue. The investor question is whether additional activity produces enough cash to fund expansion and shareholder payments. Construction delays, higher borrowing costs or weaker volumes can reduce that cash even when reported revenue grows.
sections.heading: 8) ONEOK: focus on cash from the network

sections.text:

sections.heading: 9) Baker Hughes: separate a framework from firm orders

title: October 28, 2026 earnings watch: Microsoft, Alphabet and the return on AI spending

sections.heading: 1) The schedule and forecasts to know
sections.text:
October 28, 2026 · After close

Microsoft is scheduled to release fiscal first-quarter 2027 results; Alphabet, ServiceNow, T-Mobile and O’Reilly are scheduled to release third-quarter 2026 results. KLA is scheduled to release fiscal first-quarter 2027 results. Fortinet and Equinix have confirmed third-quarter calls after close, with results expected that evening. O’Reilly’s discussion follows on October 29 during trading.

Revenue consensus checked on October 28 was about $90.62 billion for Microsoft and $127.97 billion for Alphabet. These are analyst forecasts, not reported results, and can change before release.

sections.heading: 2) Cloud and software: turn AI use into earnings
sections.text:
Microsoft earns money from cloud computing, software subscriptions and other products; Alphabet combines advertising with cloud and other businesses. Watch cloud growth alongside infrastructure spending and cash flow, because rising sales can coexist with heavier investment.

ServiceNow sells software that manages business workflows. Its October 27 Google Cloud announcement combines live integrations with others still planned. The investment question is whether the partnership produces additional subscriptions, rather than treating every planned feature as revenue already earned.

IBM’s October 21 third-quarter report offers recent enterprise-spending context: software revenue rose 8%, while consulting revenue was flat. That difference makes the mix of demand important when judging another company’s headline growth.

sections.heading: 3) Chip equipment and data centers: spending must become sales
sections.text:
KLA supplies inspection and measurement equipment used in semiconductor manufacturing. Watch customer investment plans, service demand and export restrictions. ASML reported €11.7 billion in third-quarter sales on October 14, but its lithography equipment serves a different role; that is sector context rather than a forecast for KLA.

Equinix sells data-center space, power and connections. Watch how new capacity turns into recurring revenue and cash generation after expansion spending. Strong demand alone cannot settle the timing or cost of building that capacity.

sections.heading: 4) Security and wireless: look beyond the customer count
sections.text:
Fortinet sells network-security products and services. Compare product demand with recurring service growth and the next outlook; a shift in that mix can change profitability even when total revenue rises.

T-Mobile sells wireless service and devices. Judge customer additions alongside service revenue, customer retention, promotional costs and cash flow. Verizon’s October 26 third-quarter results illustrate why the distinction matters: service revenue grew while equipment revenue declined. Its raised outlook is a competitor’s result, not a guarantee for T-Mobile.

sections.heading: 5) Auto parts: sales growth needs a margin check
sections.text:
O’Reilly sells replacement parts to repair shops and motorists. Sales at existing stores help distinguish demand from growth driven by opening more locations; margins show how much of those sales reaches profit.

Genuine Parts reported 4.2% third-quarter sales growth on October 20 but narrowed its full-year adjusted profit-per-share range to $7.50–$7.75 from $7.50–$8.00. Its mix includes industrial parts and international operations, so use that report as a prompt to check demand and costs, rather than a direct prediction for O’Reilly.

sections.heading: 6) How to read the results
sections.text:
Start with revenue, then check profit, cash flow and the updated outlook. Keep adjusted profit measures separate from standard accounting results, and compare forecasts on the same basis.

The next meaningful development is what management says about future demand and spending. Earnings can produce sharp price changes in either direction; a favorable headline does not guarantee a lasting gain.

summary: Amazon and Intel lead the earnings reports expected after close on October 29, 2026. Watch whether cloud and chip growth generate cash, while Starbucks, Mondelez and Republic Services show how demand and costs are shaping profits.

sections.text:
These reports are expected after close on October 29, 2026. The companies have announced reporting dates or earnings calls for that evening. Amazon, Intel, Gilead, Stryker, Mondelez and Republic Services are reporting their third quarters of 2026. sections.heading: 1) When are the reports, and what is expected?

sections.text:
Amazon earns money from online retail, advertising and cloud services. Cloud growth is especially important because it helps fund the data centers needed for artificial intelligence. The useful comparison is growth in cloud profit against spending on buildings, servers and equipment.

Watch free cash flow—the cash left after operating expenses and capital spending—and management’s next investment plan. A strong sales quarter can still leave less cash for shareholders if construction and equipment spending rise faster. The earnings call needs to show how new capacity is becoming paying customer demand.
sections.heading: 2) Amazon: can cloud growth fund the AI buildout?

sections.text:
Intel’s second-quarter revenue rose 25%, while data-center and AI sales rose 59%. It forecast third-quarter revenue of $15.8 billion to $16.8 billion and said it was increasing investment in equipment and manufacturing space. Watch the share of chip sales retained as profit and the cash needed to expand production.

On October 26, Intel signed an agreement to acquire Classiq, which develops software for quantum computing. The proposed combination adds a longer-term opportunity, but closing conditions and commercial adoption remain risks. The current earnings decision rests more directly on chip demand, manufacturing progress and spending.
sections.heading: 3) Intel: stronger chip sales must support factory spending

sections.text:
Sandisk sells flash memory and storage products used in data centers, devices and computers. Its previous revenue forecast of $10.3 billion to $10.8 billion puts the analyst expectation near the upper end of that range. Watch whether higher sales reflect sustainable customer demand and pricing.

The next-quarter outlook should help show whether customers are continuing to commit to storage purchases. Memory pricing can move sharply as supply and demand change, so strong current profits need support from orders and disciplined capacity investment.
sections.heading: 4) Sandisk: the next storage outlook matters as much as the quarter

sections.text:
Gilead’s second-quarter HIV sales rose 12%, while cell-therapy sales fell 14% amid competition. Acquisition-related research charges also affected earnings. Watch underlying medicine sales, operating cash flow and the cost of bringing acquired treatments to market.

Stryker sells surgical equipment and medical devices. Procedure demand, product mix and expenses will determine how much sales growth reaches profit. Boston Scientific’s October 28 report showed sales growth of 1.5% and discussed disruption from a cybersecurity incident. That is useful context for reading device earnings: company-specific execution can matter as much as demand for procedures.
sections.heading: 5) Gilead and Stryker: separate demand from company-specific costs

sections.text:
Starbucks’ previous quarter showed global comparable-store sales growth of 7.9%, including 4.2% more transactions. title: Earnings ahead: watch Amazon’s operating profit and Sandisk’s pricing power
summary: Ahead of the October 29, 2026 evening earnings reports, watch the quality of Amazon’s profit, Sandisk’s pricing strength and Starbucks’ customer recovery. Intel, healthcare and waste-service results add tests of spending and costs.

sections.heading: 1) What reports are expected after close on October 29?
sections.text:
Amazon, Intel, Gilead, Stryker, Mondelez and Republic Services are scheduled to discuss their third-quarter 2026 results this evening. Sandisk’s report covers its first quarter of fiscal 2027; Starbucks reports its fourth quarter and full fiscal year 2026. Issuer announcements confirm the evening reporting dates or calls.

The investor decision goes beyond whether sales beat expectations: distinguish profit from the underlying business, investment gains, acquisition charges and changes in how revenue is reported.

sections.heading: 2) Amazon: look past investment gains to cloud and retail profit
sections.text:
Amazon’s second-quarter net income included $53.4 billion of non-operating pretax income, mainly from its Anthropic investment. That helps explain why the next headline profit number needs a closer look. Operating income shows what its retail, advertising and cloud businesses earn before those investment effects.

In that quarter, AWS sales grew 37%, while free cash flow over the preceding twelve months was negative $7.6 billion, largely because equipment spending rose. Free cash flow is operating cash left after capital spending. Watch AWS operating profit, the new spending plan and how quickly added capacity begins serving paying customers.

Microsoft’s October 28 report showed Azure revenue growth of 48%. That provides fresh evidence of strong cloud demand, but Azure and AWS have different businesses and revenue bases. Amazon still needs to demonstrate its own growth and returns.

sections.heading: 3) Intel: test the manufacturing recovery against the spending bill
sections.text:
Intel’s July outlook put third-quarter revenue at $15.8 billion to $16.8 billion, with diluted profit per share of $0.31 under standard accounting and $0.38 after company adjustments. These are management forecasts, not reported results or analyst estimates.

Intel said better factory yields and production speed helped its second quarter, and that it was increasing equipment and manufacturing investment. Watch whether those improvements support gross margin—the share of sales left after production costs—and how much cash the expansion needs.

The October 26 agreement to acquire quantum-software company Classiq adds a longer-term opportunity. The companies remain separate until closing, expected in the first half of 2027 and subject to approvals. That agreement does not establish current-quarter revenue from the combined business.

sections.heading: 4) Sandisk: separate higher prices from higher shipment volumes
sections.text:
Sandisk’s previous quarter showed sequential revenue growth of 51%, with roughly one-third from volume and two-thirds from pricing. The distinction matters: price increases can lift profit quickly, but their durability depends on supply and customer demand.

Its prior forecast for the quarter being reported was $10.3 billion to $10.8 billion in revenue. The analyst revenue expectation as of October 29 is about $10.72 billion, near the upper end. Watch the next sales and margin outlook, data-center demand and whether customers continue buying at higher prices. This report is for fiscal first-quarter 2027, not a calendar third-quarter comparison.

sections.heading: 5) Gilead: separate medicine demand from acquisition effects
sections.text:
Gilead’s second-quarter HIV product sales grew 12%, and operating cash flow was $3.6 billion. Acquisition-related research charges also drove a large reported loss. For the next report, read medicine sales and cash generation alongside the explanation of those charges.

The company sells treatments across HIV, liver disease and oncology. Watch whether its main medicines keep funding new products and acquired research, rather than judging the business only by a rebound in headline profit. Competition and the cost of developing treatments remain important risks.

sections.heading: 6) Stryker: does the recovery keep reaching profit?
sections.text:
Stryker’s July report described recovery from a cyber incident and showed 9.0% organic sales growth, largely from more units sold. Organic growth removes currency and acquisition effects. Its adjusted operating margin reached 27.4%, up 1.7 percentage points.

The device maker’s next results should show whether surgical equipment and implant demand continue translating into profit. Watch manufacturing and service execution as well as procedure demand; recovery costs or disruption could weaken the share of sales retained as earnings.

sections.heading: 7) Starbucks: compare customer recovery with its own target

sections.heading: 8) Mondelez: can snack volumes strengthen earnings?

sections.heading: 9) Republic Services: follow pricing through to cash

sections.heading: 3) Williams and Diamondback: two different energy cash-flow tests

summary: AMD and Arista put AI spending in focus after close on November 3. Amgen, Booking, Block, AIG, Prudential and IFF add tests of drug growth, travel demand and financial resilience.

sections.heading: 1) What is scheduled for November 3?

This is a preview of the decisions ahead. AIG, IFF and Prudential plan their results calls for November 4, so their written releases and management discussions arrive on different days.

sections.heading: 2) AMD: can faster sales support profit margins?
sections.text:
AMD’s August 4 outlook called for third-quarter revenue of $13 billion, plus or minus $300 million, and an adjusted gross margin of about 56%. Gross margin is the share of sales left after the direct cost of products. Compare the coming results with that company outlook and watch whether the next-quarter forecast shows continued demand for data-center chips.

sections.heading: 3) Arista: will new AI networking products become sales?
sections.text:
Arista announced rack-scale Ethernet systems on October 7, developed with partners including AMD, Broadcom and major cloud customers. These systems connect large groups of AI chips. The earnings question is how product launches translate into customer spending, shipment timing and profit margins.

Watch the revenue outlook and customer concentration. Large buyers can create substantial orders, but shifts in their spending plans can also make quarterly growth uneven.

sections.heading: 4) Amgen: how does recent cancer-drug progress change the outlook?
sections.text:
On October 24, Amgen reported interim Phase 3 results for Imdelltra combined with Imfinzi in a specific first-line maintenance lung-cancer setting. The combination reduced the measured risk of death by 58% versus Imfinzi alone in that trial. This is clinical evidence, rather than a guarantee of future sales or expanded approval.

For earnings, watch current medicine sales, pricing and research spending. Management’s discussion of the route from trial results to potential use in this treatment setting matters alongside the quarterly profit figures.

sections.heading: 5) Booking: is stronger hotel demand reaching the travel platform?
sections.text:
Booking earns revenue through online travel reservations and related services. Watch room nights, the value of bookings and marketing spending to see whether demand is becoming profitable growth.

Marriott reported on November 2 that third-quarter revenue per available room rose 6.5% worldwide in constant currencies, and raised its full-year growth outlook to 4.5%–5%. Revenue per available room combines hotel occupancy and room pricing. This is useful travel-sector context, but hotel operators and online booking platforms earn money differently.

sections.heading: 6) Block: does the seller ecosystem produce profitable growth?
sections.text:
Marqeta announced on October 19 that it is powering Square’s business credit card on the American Express network, bringing Square’s debit, prepaid and credit programs onto one processing platform. This is an operating development to assess alongside earnings, rather than a quantified promise of new profit.

Watch Square seller activity, Cash App engagement and gross profit, together with operating costs and credit losses. More borrowing can deepen customer relationships, but it also increases the importance of repayment quality.

sections.heading: 7) AIG: can expansion preserve insurance profitability?
sections.text:
On October 30, AIG announced a signed agreement to buy Everest’s Chile insurance business and completed the separate Colombia acquisition. The Chile transaction remains subject to approvals and is expected to close in the first half of 2027.

Watch the combined ratio, which compares claims and expenses with insurance premiums. A ratio below 100% indicates an underwriting profit before investment income. Premium growth is more valuable when pricing also covers claims, expenses and catastrophe risk.

sections.heading: 8) Prudential: what has already been disclosed?
sections.text:
Prudential’s October 15 filing estimated that its Japan sales suspension reduced third-quarter pre-tax adjusted operating income by about $140 million. It also disclosed $1.47 trillion of PGIM assets under management at September 30. These were preliminary figures, and the full earnings release remains a separate event.

Watch the final Japan impact, investment-management fees and insurance earnings. Segment reporting has changed, so compare the revised historical figures when judging growth. Interest rates, markets and investment losses can affect results.

sections.heading: 9) IFF: how profitable is the smaller continuing business?
sections.text:
IFF’s August 4 report presented Food Ingredients as discontinued operations after a signed agreement to sell that business. The sale was expected to close by the end of the second quarter of 2027, subject to conditions. It had not been described as completed in that report.

Watch sales and margins in the continuing business, together with costs that remain after a sale. Compare like-for-like results: removing a business can reduce reported revenue without showing that the remaining products are selling less.

sections.heading: 10) How should investors read the results?
sections.text:
Start with revenue, cash generation and the outlook for the next period. EPS means profit per share; adjusted EPS removes selected costs and can differ substantially from profit under GAAP accounting rules.

Compare each measure on the same basis and fiscal period. A strong past quarter can still be followed by a cautious outlook, and share prices can move sharply after close when trading is thinner. The most useful next step is to check what changed in the business and whether management’s outlook supports it.

sections.heading: 2) What changed before this report?

At its September 23 investor presentation, McDonald’s outlined franchisee support through rent relief and capital contributions, including about $5 billion through 2030. It also targeted an operating profit margin in the low-to-mid 50% range by 2030. These are future plans and targets.

The decision now is whether near-term spending can improve service and customer visits enough to strengthen longer-term cash returns. Look for measurable progress rather than treating a technology rollout as an immediate earnings benefit.

A sustained hold above $253 would support the recovery. A close below $247 would weaken it. These chart zones describe past trading; an earnings surprise can move the stock through them.

sections.heading: 4) How the business makes money
sections.text: McDonald’s earns rent and royalties from franchised restaurants and records sales from restaurants it operates itself. About 95% of locations are independently operated. That is an observed reaction, not a forecast for McDonald’s. Chipotle operates its restaurants more directly, so their profit margins are not interchangeable.

sections.heading: 7) Risks into the report
sections.text: Discounts can lift sales while squeezing restaurant profit. Food and labor costs, weak consumer spending, currency changes and disruption during upgrades can offset efficiency gains. Support for franchisees also uses cash before its benefits are fully visible.

title: Parker earnings preview for November 5: filtration deal puts organic growth in focus

sections.heading: 1) When are earnings, and what is expected?
sections.text:
Parker has confirmed its first-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings for November 5, 2026 before open. The quarter ended September 30. Parker’s fiscal year ends in June, so this is fiscal 2027 despite taking place in calendar 2026.

MarketBeat estimates reviewed November 3 were $8.21 of adjusted profit per share and approximately $5.81 billion of sales. These are analyst expectations, not reported results. Compare the actual profit with the same adjusted definition when results arrive.

sections.heading: 2) Will acquired sales translate into profit?
sections.text:
Parker closed its Filtration Group acquisition on August 13. Management expected approximately $1.8 billion of added fiscal 2027 sales over 10.5 months of ownership, with about 60% in North American industrial operations and 40% internationally. The deal was expected to be neutral to adjusted EPS in the first quarter and increase adjusted EPS over the full year.

That creates two separate tests: how the existing businesses are performing, and how the acquired business contributes after financing and integration costs. The August 6 annual outlook excluded Filtration Group while it was pending. A higher sales outlook after including the acquisition would not, by itself, demonstrate faster organic growth.

sections.heading: 3) What do the recent results and charts show?
sections.text:
In the June quarter, Parker reported $5.755 billion of sales, GAAP diluted EPS of $8.54 and adjusted EPS of $9.27. GAAP follows standard accounting rules; adjusted profit removes selected items. Organic sales grew 8%, while adjusted segment operating margin reached 28%. Margin measures the share of sales left as operating profit.

The shares closed November 2 at $928.29, below their 20-day average of $937.77 and 50-day average of $954.56. Recent trading provides approximate reference areas of $868–$900 and $938–$955. A close above $955 would improve the recent setup; a close below $868 would weaken the recent low area. These are reference points, and earnings can move the stock beyond them.

sections.heading: 4) How the business makes money
sections.text: Parker makes motion and control components used in industrial equipment, transportation and aerospace. Its products include hydraulic, pneumatic, sealing, filtration and fluid-control technologies. It earns sales from original equipment and replacement parts, so factory activity, aircraft production and maintenance demand all matter. The financial image shows the fiscal year ended June 30, before Filtration Group joined the company.

sections.heading: 5) What to watch
sections.text:
The main decision is whether organic demand and margins support the next annual outlook as Filtration Group joins reported sales. Parker’s August baseline projected 5.5%–8.5% organic sales growth and adjusted EPS of $34.25–$35.25 for fiscal 2027, excluding the then-pending acquisitions. Watch management distinguish acquisition contributions from underlying growth.

The Filtration Group closing announcement also targeted approximately $220 million of pre-tax cost savings by the end of year three. Those are management targets, rather than achieved savings. Cash generation and debt reduction will help investors judge whether the acquisition creates value after its costs.

sections.heading: 6) Recently reported peers
sections.text:
RTX reported its third quarter on October 20. Sales were $24.965 billion, GAAP EPS was $1.89 and adjusted EPS was $2.26. That price window includes all developments affecting the shares that day.

sections.text: A slowdown in industrial orders or aircraft production can reduce sales and factory efficiency. Acquisition integration, financing costs and delays in expected savings can hurt profit even when reported sales rise. sections.text:
The central question is whether strong U.S. customer demand keeps turning into revenue without a comparable rise in delivery costs. Watch commercial sales growth, expansion by existing customers and the next annual outlook.

At the August report, management raised its full-year revenue range to $8.150 billion–$8.158 billion from $7.650 billion–$7.662 billion. sections.heading: 2) What would show that growth is becoming durable?

sections.text:
On October 19, Palantir and Knox announced a partnership focused on secure software delivery to U.S. government customers. It is intended to make deployment in regulated federal environments faster and easier. No quantified revenue contribution was disclosed in that announcement.

An October 1 partnership with Armada also targets AI systems that customers can run on infrastructure they control. These initiatives could broaden the routes to customers. The earnings test is whether deployment opportunities become paying usage and revenue; an announced partnership is not the same as recognized sales.
sections.heading: 3) What changed in the partnership pipeline?

sections.text:
Palantir exceeded the dated profit and revenue forecasts in both of its latest completed quarters. Yet the stock fell about 6.9% from the May 4 pre-release close to the May 5 close, then rose about 29.5% from the August 3 pre-release close to the August 4 close.

At the October 28 close, the stock traded at about 168 times trailing reported profit per share and 76.8 times trailing sales. Those ratios use results through June 30, 2026. A high valuation makes the future growth outlook important even when the current quarter exceeds forecasts.
sections.heading: 4) Why can the stock react differently to two earnings beats?

sections.text:
The October 28 regular close of $196.81 was just below its 20-day price average of $197.16 and above its 50-day average of $186.28. The momentum indicator RSI was about 53.9 on a 0–100 scale. ATR, a measure of typical daily price range, was about $7.69.

title: Southern earnings preview for November 5: power demand meets a funding test
summary: Southern’s November 5 earnings will test whether growing power demand supports its annual profit outlook without straining financing. OpenAI’s new grid-flexibility program adds context to Georgia Power’s approved data-center contract.

sections.heading: 1) When is the report, and what is expected?
sections.text:
Southern has confirmed its third-quarter 2026 earnings release for November 5 before open. The quarter ended September 30. Analyst estimates from MarketBeat reviewed November 3 were adjusted profit per share of $1.71 and operating revenue of approximately $8.38 billion. These are expectations, not reported results.

The company’s July outlook retained annual adjusted EPS of $4.50–$4.60 while targeting near or at the top of that range. Compare any November change with the same annual period and adjusted profit definition.

sections.heading: 2) Does more electricity demand mean better earnings?
sections.text:
Southern reported second-quarter adjusted basic EPS of $1.13 and GAAP diluted EPS of $1.03. GAAP follows standard accounting rules; the adjusted figure excludes selected items, including costs tied to replacing equipment at wind facilities. Revenue was $6.977 billion, close to the prior-year level, while adjusted profit benefited from utility investment, customer usage and growth, lower income taxes and equity investments. Higher interest expense partly offset those gains.

First-half retail electricity sales grew 2.3% after adjusting for weather. Watch demand that turns into billed usage and investments that regulators permit the utilities to recover from customers. Revenue can also change when fuel costs are passed through to customers, so faster sales growth does not automatically mean the same improvement in profit.

sections.heading: 3) What does the recent share-price trend show?
sections.text:
Southern closed November 2 at $94.61, above its 20-day average of $90.16 and 50-day average of $87.90. Recent trading provides approximate reference areas of $89–$91.30 and $93.80–$94.90. A close above $94.90 would clear the recent high area; a close below $89 would weaken the recent low area. Earnings can move the shares outside these ranges.

The comparison image shows a gain of about 3.4% between the April 29 and April 30 closes and a decline of about 1.8% between the July 29 and July 30 closes. Those windows followed before-open results and include all news affecting the shares each day.

sections.heading: 4) How the business makes money
sections.text: Southern owns electric utilities in Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi, natural-gas distribution businesses and other energy operations. Regulated utilities earn approved returns on eligible investment while collecting customer revenue for service and recovering certain costs. Regulators decide which spending can be recovered, so construction, customer affordability and financing matter alongside demand. The financial image uses consolidated revenue categories, with internal transactions removed.

sections.heading: 5) What to watch
sections.text:
OpenAI launched its Grid Protectors Program on November 2, highlighting its planned Effingham County campus. Its existing Georgia Power agreement includes up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand: the facility would reduce electricity use when the grid is strained. Georgia Power announced regulatory approval of the contract in August and described 3,200 megawatts of future demand, with OpenAI paying the infrastructure costs required to serve it. The campus remains in development.

This matters because customer contracts can affect how much capacity the utility must build and who pays for it. Watch Southern distinguish contracted future demand from operating customer usage, and update the timing of infrastructure investment. Its July presentation identified $700 million of additional equity funding arranged in the quarter and $1.1 billion of remaining projected equity needs for its base plan. New investment opportunities may require further financing.

sections.heading: 6) Recently reported peers
sections.text:
NextEra Energy reported its third quarter on October 21. Operating revenue was $8.09 billion, GAAP EPS was $2.28 and adjusted EPS was $1.24. Compared with the dated consensus in the image, adjusted profit beat by about 3.3%, while revenue missed by about 4.5%. NextEra retained annual adjusted EPS guidance of $3.92–$4.02 and targeted the high end.

Florida Power & Light’s regulatory capital employed grew about 9.2%, illustrating how approved investment can support utility earnings. NextEra also owns a large competitive energy business, and its GAAP profit included financial-hedging gains. Its mix and accounting effects differ from Southern’s. NextEra shares fell about 0.7% between the October 20 and October 21 closes; that is an observed price reaction, rather than proof of a single cause.

sections.heading: 7) Risks into the report
sections.text: Customer projects may be delayed or use less electricity than expected. Utilities can face higher debt costs, additional share issuance, construction overruns and limits on recovering costs through rates. Severe weather can disrupt service and create restoration expenses, while mild weather can reduce usage. Regulation and affordability concerns can change project timing and allowed returns.

Coca-Cola confirms third-quarter results before open on October 27. It sells beverages through a global brand and bottling system. Watch whether higher sales come from more drinks sold or higher prices, and whether currency movements help or hurt reported revenue. More pricing can support profit while putting pressure on demand.

Visa confirms fiscal fourth-quarter and full-year results after close on October 27. Its payments network earns fees as money moves between customers, merchants and financial institutions. Watch payment volumes, international transactions and the next fiscal-year outlook. Visa and Mastercard provide useful comparisons, but their fees and reporting periods differ.

sections.heading: 3) Wednesday, October 28: Microsoft and Alphabet
sections.text:
Microsoft confirms fiscal first-quarter 2027 results after close on October 28. It earns money from software, subscriptions and cloud services. Watch Azure cloud growth, demand for AI services and whether investment in computing capacity leaves enough cash after spending. Strong demand does not guarantee that each new dollar of revenue will be equally profitable.

Alphabet confirms third-quarter results on October 28 before its earnings call. The notice does not state the release time. Advertising supports much of the business, alongside Google Cloud and subscriptions. Watch search advertising, cloud profit and the cost of AI infrastructure. Meta is a useful advertising peer, but its social apps and legal costs make its profit figures different from Alphabet’s.

sections.heading: 4) Thursday, October 29: Amazon and Intel
sections.text:
Amazon confirms its third-quarter earnings call for October 29, but its notice does not state the release time; an after-close release is expected. Retail, advertising and Amazon Web Services provide different sources of sales and profit. Watch cloud demand, retail operating profit and the holiday-quarter outlook. Heavy investment can reduce available cash even when sales grow.

Intel confirms third-quarter results after close on October 29. It designs processors and invests in factories that also aim to serve outside chip customers. Watch demand for PC and server chips, factory costs and evidence of progress in manufacturing. Customer interest and future plans should be distinguished from booked revenue and profitable production.

sections.heading: 5) Thursday, October 29: Lilly, Mastercard and Caterpillar
sections.text:
Lilly confirms third-quarter results on October 29; a before-open release is expected. Watch Mounjaro and Zepbound sales, production capacity and the full-year outlook. Its August 5 second-quarter release raised annual revenue guidance to $85–87 billion. Research acquisition charges can materially affect profit per share, so changes in those charges need to be separated from medicine demand.

Mastercard confirms third-quarter results on October 29 ahead of a call before open. Watch spending on its payments network, international travel-related transactions and growth in services. Its results can add context to Visa’s earlier report, while differences in business mix limit direct comparisons.

Caterpillar confirms third-quarter results before open on October 29. Construction and mining equipment, engines and power systems connect it to several investment cycles. Watch customer demand, dealer inventories, costs and the outlook. Higher sales do not by themselves show whether customers are buying more equipment or dealers are rebuilding inventory.

sections.heading: 6) Friday, October 30: ExxonMobil, Chevron and AbbVie
sections.text:
ExxonMobil confirms third-quarter results before open on October 30. Chevron confirms its third-quarter call on October 30; its advisory does not state a release time, and a before-open release is expected. Both sell oil and gas and operate refining businesses. Compare production, the profit earned from refining, cash generation and spending before judging dividends or buybacks. Commodity prices and business mix can produce different outcomes even for these close peers.

AbbVie confirms third-quarter results before open on October 30. Watch demand for its immunology medicines, the wider product portfolio and its outlook. An October 5 filing put third-quarter adjusted profit guidance at $3.73–3.77 per share after including research acquisition and milestone costs. This is company guidance, not reported earnings or analyst consensus.

sections.heading: 7) What recently reported peers tell us
sections.text:
Meta reported third-quarter results on October 21: revenue was $64.60 billion, up 26%, and reported diluted profit was $3.83 per share. A $9.89 billion legal-settlement charge affected profit. The useful lesson for Alphabet and the cloud companies is to examine demand, costs and investment separately; Meta’s results do not predict their results.

PepsiCo reported third-quarter results on October 8. Revenue grew 5.6% to $25.27 billion, while organic revenue grew 3.1%; organic growth removes currency and portfolio changes. Its core operating margin, an adjusted measure of operating profit as a share of sales, fell to 16.9% from 17.3%. That makes sales volume, pricing and costs useful questions for Coca-Cola, while PepsiCo’s snack business limits a direct comparison.

sections.heading: 8) Prepare for the outlook as well as the quarter
sections.text: Read the next-quarter or full-year outlook alongside the reported quarter. Separate recurring business performance from investment gains, legal charges and research acquisition costs. None of the upcoming figures in this report are announced results. Dates and expectations can change, and a positive earnings surprise does not guarantee a rising stock price. title: Top Market Events to Watch This Week (November 2–6, 2026 | U.S. Eastern Time)
summary: Jobs data, U.S. midterm elections and business surveys shape the week, alongside Apple, AMD and other earnings. Watch how demand, costs and company guidance change the outlook for stock prices.

sections.text:
The clearest test of whether hiring can support spending without adding inflation pressure.
📅 Friday, November 6 — 8:30 AM ET
What it is: The monthly report covers payroll jobs, unemployment and hourly wages. The November 1 calendar forecast is for 55,000 additional jobs and 4.2% unemployment; revisions to earlier months also matter.
Impact:
• Steady hiring with softer wage growth could ease interest-rate pressure while preserving demand, supporting growth stocks and consumer businesses.
• Much stronger hiring or wages could lift bond yields and pressure expensive technology shares. A sharp hiring slowdown could instead hurt retailers and banks through weaker spending and credit quality.
sections.heading: 1) Employment Situation — October jobs and wages

sections.text:
The results could change expectations for taxes, regulation and federal spending.
📅 Tuesday, November 3 — voting hours vary by state; results may extend into later days.
What it is: Federal elections determine the next House and the Senate seats being contested. Congressional control influences which policy proposals can advance; an election result is not an enacted law.
Impact:
• A clearer path for a specific tax or spending proposal could help its likely beneficiaries, such as companies exposed to infrastructure or government contracts, if the proposal advances.
• A divided Congress or close, unresolved races could delay policy changes and keep uncertainty elevated. Healthcare, energy and financial shares may react differently as investors reassess regulation.
sections.heading: 2) U.S. midterm elections — control of Congress

sections.text:
A broad business survey that connects consumer demand with service-sector costs.
📅 Wednesday, November 4 — 10:00 AM ET
What it is: Purchasing managers describe October activity, new orders, employment and prices. PMI means purchasing managers’ index; a reading above 50 indicates expansion within the surveyed sector. The November 1 calendar forecast is 54.6.
Impact:
• Healthy orders with easing prices could support travel, payments and consumer-service stocks while reducing concern about persistent inflation.
• Higher prices could push yields up even if activity is strong. Weak orders could lower sales expectations for service businesses and suppliers.
sections.heading: 3) ISM Services PMI — demand and price pressure

sections.text:
An early check on industrial demand and the outlook for companies tied to investment.
📅 Monday, November 2 — 10:00 AM ET
What it is: The October survey tracks factory activity, new orders, employment and input prices. The November 1 calendar forecast is 54.5. Orders and prices together help explain whether stronger activity is likely to improve profits.
Impact:
• Stronger orders with controlled costs could support machinery, industrial suppliers and transport shares by improving their sales outlook.
• Falling orders could pressure cyclical stocks, whose earnings depend heavily on economic growth. Rising input prices could squeeze manufacturers’ margins even if production expands.
sections.heading: 4) ISM Manufacturing PMI — factory orders and costs

sections.text:
An advance clue to employers’ willingness to hire before Friday’s jobs report.
📅 Tuesday, November 3 — 10:00 AM ET
What it is: The Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey covers September vacancies, hiring, quits and layoffs. The November 1 calendar forecast is 7.1 million openings. Vacancies are not the same as completed hires.
Impact:
• A gradual decline in vacancies without a jump in layoffs could ease wage pressure, helping rate-sensitive technology and housing shares.
• A steep drop in hiring could signal weaker demand and hurt staffing or consumer stocks. An unexpected rise in vacancies could revive concern about wage inflation and lift yields.
sections.heading: 5) JOLTS — job openings and labor demand

sections.text:
Jobs, business demand and election results are the main market tests for November 2–6, 2026. Tuesday brings labor-demand data and voting; Friday’s jobs report could change expectations for interest rates and consumer spending.

The most supportive combination would be resilient demand, easing cost pressure and company forecasts that hold up. Strong growth with rising yields could still weigh on highly valued shares; weaker growth could hurt earnings even if borrowing costs fall.

Company guidance provides a second check. AI-related businesses need to show that investment becomes profitable sales, while consumer businesses need to show that promotions attract customers without eroding margins.
sections.heading: 6) Overall Market Theme This Week

sections.text:
All dates below refer to U.S. Eastern Time. Confirmed dates come from company announcements; expected windows remain estimates where the notice does not establish the release session.

Monday, November 2 — after close
Apple (AAPL), fiscal fourth quarter: expected reporting window on the earnings calendar. Apple earns money from devices and services. Watch the holiday sales outlook, product mix and gross margin—the share of sales left after product costs. Strong demand helps only if component costs and supply constraints leave enough profit.

Palantir (PLTR), third quarter: issuer-confirmed after close. Its software serves commercial and government customers. Watch U.S. commercial sales, contract conversion and cash generation; delayed projects and a high valuation increase sensitivity to a weaker outlook.

Tuesday, November 3 — before open
Eaton (ETN), third quarter: issuer-confirmed before open. Electrical equipment and power-management products make its orders a useful check on data-center investment. Watch backlog conversion and margins; capacity expansion and project delays can consume cash before sales arrive.

Pfizer (PFE), third quarter: issuer-confirmed Tuesday morning; the before-open window is expected. Its medicines and vaccines business faces decisions about product growth, development spending and future revenue as patents expire. Watch the annual outlook and cash generation; clinical setbacks and pricing pressure remain material risks.

Marathon Petroleum (MPC), third quarter: issuer-confirmed date, with before open expected. Refining and fuel logistics make profit sensitive to the difference between crude costs and refined-product prices. Watch refining margins, maintenance and cash returns; higher crude prices alone do not guarantee stronger refining earnings.

Tuesday, November 3 — after close
AMD (AMD), fiscal third quarter: issuer-confirmed after close. Processors and AI accelerators connect its outlook to cloud and enterprise spending. Watch data-center sales, the next-quarter outlook and gross margin; competition, export limits and product delivery can change how much demand becomes profit.

Arista Networks (ANET), third quarter: issuer-confirmed after close. Its network switches connect data-center computing equipment. Watch AI networking sales and operating profitability; dependence on a few large customers makes shifts in their spending consequential.

Amgen (AMGN), third quarter: issuer-confirmed after close. Its medicines business depends on product volumes, net prices and successful development. Watch growth medicines and the annual outlook; competition, development costs and debt can limit cash available to shareholders.

Wednesday, November 4 — before open expected
Uber (UBER), third quarter: expected reporting window. Its platform earns money from rides, delivery and related services. Watch bookings—the value of transactions on the platform—and cash generation. Its August 5 outlook called for third-quarter bookings of $58.25 billion–$60.25 billion; incentives, competition and regulation can affect how much becomes profit.

McDonald’s (MCD), third quarter: expected date and before-open window. Franchise fees, rent and restaurant sales connect its outlook to consumer spending. Watch customer visits and the cost of value offers; discounts can attract diners while reducing restaurant profit.

Wednesday, November 4 — after close
Qualcomm (QCOM), fiscal fourth quarter and full year: issuer-confirmed after close. Chips and patent licensing fund the business. Watch handset demand, automotive diversification and the next outlook; customer concentration and competition can offset gains in newer markets.

Thursday, November 5 — before open
ConocoPhillips (COP), third quarter: issuer-confirmed before open. Oil and gas production links its cash flow to realized energy prices, output and costs. Watch spending discipline and cash after investment; commodity-price declines and operational disruption can reduce shareholder returns.

Recent peer context
ServiceNow’s October 28 third-quarter release reported $4.106 billion of revenue and raised its annual subscription-revenue outlook. That is useful enterprise-software demand context for Palantir, although their customers and contracts differ.

Chipotle’s October 28 third-quarter results showed comparable restaurant sales up 2.1%, while operating margin fell to 13.7% from 15.9%. For McDonald’s, the useful question is whether better traffic also improves profit; the franchise and company-operated models differ.

ExxonMobil’s October 30 third-quarter release reported profit per share of $3.72, or $4.23 after its stated adjustments. Its refining operations provide context for Marathon, while its production business provides context for ConocoPhillips. Their business mixes differ, so the result does not predict either company’s earnings.
sections.heading: 7) Earnings to Watch This Week

sections.text:
Before a major release, some investors reduce positions or buy protection. That can affect prices, but it does not create a dependable pattern of selling before the event and rallying afterward.

After the release, compare the outcome with expectations, then watch bond yields and company guidance. Strong data can hurt share valuations if yields rise; weak data can hurt profits even if investors expect lower rates.

Prices can reverse as details and revisions are absorbed. A put option can provide downside exposure, but a purchased option can lose its entire cost; a correct directional view may still lose money if the move is too small or too late.
sections.heading: 8) How Traders Typically Approach These Events

sections.text:
• Compare each result with what investors expected, including revisions and the company’s next forecast.
• Watch bond yields alongside earnings: financing costs and future profit both influence stock prices.
• Treat the scenarios as a watchlist for decisions, and size positions for outcomes that may go either way.

title: This Week’s Market Forecast: Your Day-by-Day Outlook (November 9–13, 2026 | U.S. Eastern Time)
summary:
Tuesday’s CPI and Friday’s producer prices test the inflation outlook.

sections.heading: 1) Consumer Price Index (CPI): October inflation
sections.text:
This is the week’s clearest test of whether inflation is easing.

📅 Tuesday, November 10 — 8:30 AM ET

What it is: CPI measures consumer prices; core CPI excludes food and energy to help reveal underlying inflation.

Impact:
• Softer inflation than expected could lower bond yields and support technology stocks by reducing the interest rates used to value future profits.
• Hotter inflation could lift yields and pressure expensive growth stocks, even if company earnings remain strong.

sections.heading: 2) Producer Price Index (PPI): October inflation
sections.text:
Producer prices help reveal cost pressures facing businesses.

📅 Friday, November 13 — 8:30 AM ET

What it is: PPI tracks prices received by domestic producers, offering a different view of inflation from consumer prices.

Impact:
• Slower price increases could ease concerns about future inflation and support businesses whose costs are falling.
• A hotter report could raise concerns about squeezed margins or higher consumer prices, weighing on rate-sensitive stocks.

sections.heading: 3) Weekly jobless claims
sections.text:
Claims provide a timely check on layoffs and household income.

📅 Thursday, November 12 — 8:30 AM ET

What it is: Initial claims count new applications for unemployment benefits, with this report covering the week ended November 7.

Impact:
• Low claims could support confidence in spending and company sales, although a very tight labor market may keep interest-rate expectations high.
• A sharp rise could hurt retailers and other economically sensitive stocks by signaling weaker employment, even if bond yields fall.

sections.heading: 4) Existing-home sales: October
sections.text:
Housing turnover helps drive spending on renovation, furnishings and moving.

📅 Thursday, November 12 — 10:00 AM ET

What it is: The report counts completed sales of existing homes, rather than newly signed contracts or new construction.

Impact:
• Stronger sales could support renovation suppliers and housing-related retailers as more households move and upgrade properties.
• Weaker sales could signal that borrowing costs and affordability are restraining demand, pressuring those businesses.

sections.heading: 5) NFIB small-business optimism: October
sections.text:
Small firms provide a useful check on hiring, investment and pricing plans.

📅 Tuesday, November 10 — 6:00 AM ET

What it is: The survey combines ten measures of business conditions and expectations, including hiring and capital spending.

Impact:
• Improving sales and investment expectations could support smaller companies and suppliers that depend on domestic demand.
• Weaker hiring or expansion plans could hurt confidence in smaller companies, while rising pricing plans would add to inflation concerns.

sections.heading: 6) Overall Market Theme This Week
sections.text:
Inflation reports on Tuesday and Friday will test interest-rate expectations, while earnings from Cisco and Applied Materials will test whether AI investment is translating into profitable sales.

Cooling prices alongside resilient demand would be a supportive combination for equities; hotter inflation or deteriorating company outlooks would make that balance harder to sustain.

• Take-Two Interactive (TTWO), fiscal Q2 2027, expected after close with the earnings call confirmed that evening: the September launch of NBA 2K27 makes player spending and the game pipeline useful checkpoints for revenue, while development and marketing costs remain risks.

Tuesday, November 10 — before open

Recent peer context

Lam Research reported September-quarter revenue of $8.22 billion on October 21, up 22% from the previous quarter, supporting the case for strong chip-equipment demand ahead of Applied Materials’ own update.

Netflix’s October 20 report showed 12% revenue growth but a lower advertising outlook, a reminder ahead of Skydance’s report that streaming growth and advertising momentum can diverge.

sections.heading: 8) How Traders Typically Approach These Events
sections.text:
Investors may reduce exposure or hedge ahead of major releases, and prices can jump in either direction when results arrive. Pre-event selling and a relief rally afterward are not reliable patterns.

Strong growth data can still hurt stocks if bond yields rise, while weak data can damage profit expectations despite lower yields. If using bought options, the premium—the option price—can be lost in full, and a drop in expected volatility can reduce an option’s value after the event.

sections.heading: 9) In simple terms
sections.text:
• Compare each result with expectations, not just the previous month.
• Watch bond yields alongside company profit guidance.
• Keep position sizes manageable when the outcome is uncertain.

title: October 27, 2026 premarket: Celestica jumps, Xylem lowers outlook
summary: Celestica climbed on a $40 billion revenue outlook for 2027, while Xylem cut its profit forecast. Royal Caribbean raised guidance as investors awaited the Federal Reserve decision.

sections.heading: 1) AI growth leads the morning
sections.text:
Celestica rose 16.70% after its October 26 earnings release. The maker of data-center equipment reported third-quarter adjusted EPS, or profit per share, of $3.30 and revenue of $5.83 billion. It forecast $40 billion of revenue for 2027, compared with its $21 billion outlook for 2026.

The opportunity comes with funding demands. Celestica lowered its 2026 free cash flow forecast to $460 million from $600 million, mainly to support working capital for growth. Its 2027 capital spending forecast is $1.5 billion–$2 billion. Investors should watch how quickly customer demand turns into cash.

sections.heading: 2) Travel results show demand and cost tradeoffs
sections.text:
Royal Caribbean rose 4.42% following its October 27 third-quarter release. Revenue reached $5.6 billion and adjusted EPS was $6.57. Strong last-minute bookings and costs shifting into the fourth quarter helped results exceed company guidance. Full-year adjusted EPS is now forecast at $17.85–$17.95; higher fuel costs remain a risk.

Hilton fell 4.23% despite third-quarter adjusted EPS rising to $2.45 from $2.11 a year earlier. Its October 27 release projected fourth-quarter revenue per available room growth of 3%–3.5%, compared with 5.8% growth in the third quarter. That measure combines hotel pricing and occupancy. Hilton also cited lower expectations for its Middle East business and timeshare license fees in its full-year outlook.

sections.heading: 3) Xylem lowers its profit outlook
sections.text:
Xylem fell 5.67% before open. Its October 27 third-quarter release reported revenue of about $2.2 billion, down 3%, with project timing and more cautious customer spending weighing on sales. It cut its full-year adjusted EPS range to $5.40–$5.45 from $5.55–$5.70.

Xylem also announced plans to sell Applied Water International and Specialty Flow Control and reorganize into three segments in 2027. These are planned changes. The investor question is whether a more focused portfolio and cost savings can offset softer sales.

title: October 28, 2026 premarket: Vertiv and Flex raise outlooks; Robinhood profit slips
summary: Vertiv and Flex climbed before open after stronger results and raised outlooks. Robinhood fell as weaker crypto revenue weighed on profit, with the Federal Reserve decision still ahead.

sections.heading: 1) Outlook upgrades put data-center suppliers in focus
sections.text:
Vertiv’s third-quarter sales reached $4.31 billion, up 61%, and its adjusted operating margin rose to 25.2% from 22.3%. The power and cooling supplier raised its full-year sales forecast midpoint by $650 million to $14.65 billion. Stronger orders support the growth story; converting those orders into profitable deliveries remains the next test.

Flex reported $8.5 billion in sales for its second quarter of fiscal 2027, up 25%. Adjusted profit per share reached $1.18, versus $0.79 a year earlier. Its raised annual forecast includes recent acquisitions but excludes the planned separation of its Cloud and Power Infrastructure business. Investors therefore need to watch both operating growth and the terms of that separation.

sections.heading: 2) Healthcare and coatings raise their earnings targets
sections.text:
GE HealthCare’s third-quarter sales rose 7.2% to $5.51 billion. It increased its full-year adjusted profit-per-share forecast to $4.95–$5.05 from $4.80–$5.00. The upgrade matters because stronger sales now come with a higher annual earnings target.

PPG raised the midpoint of its full-year adjusted profit-per-share outlook, with a new range of $7.90–$8.10. Pricing and productivity helped offset inflation, though its industrial coatings business still faced pressure. The next question is whether price increases can keep protecting profit as costs change.

sections.heading: 3) Revenue growth does not guarantee a higher share price
sections.text:
Robinhood’s third-quarter revenue rose 12% to $1.42 billion, but reported profit per share fell 16% to $0.51. Crypto transaction revenue dropped 55% while operating expenses rose 16%. This is a useful reminder to check which businesses generate growth and how much of that revenue becomes profit.

F5’s fiscal fourth-quarter revenue rose 13% to $917 million, while adjusted operating margin fell to 33.7% from 37.0%. Its lower share price comes alongside a clear profitability question: can the company restore margin as sales grow?

NXP reported third-quarter sales of $3.79 billion and forecast fourth-quarter sales of $3.75 billion–$3.95 billion. CoStar raised its full-year revenue outlook to $3.75 billion–$3.77 billion. Their declines show that a strong past quarter alone does not settle what investors will pay for future earnings.

title: Tech earnings pressure stocks as stronger outlooks lift consumers and aerospace — October 29, 2026
summary: Technology stocks weakened before open on October 29 as earnings reports put cash flow and future growth under scrutiny, while stronger outlooks supported cruise, consumer and aerospace shares.

sections.text:
Alphabet’s third-quarter revenue rose 25% to $127.6 billion and Google Cloud sales more than doubled, but capital spending exceeded operating cash flow by $9.07 billion. The stock’s decline puts the next investor question on whether cloud profits can eventually fund that expansion.

Fortinet’s stronger product sales came with a lower annual services outlook. ServiceNow raised its annual targets, but forecast 18.5% growth in contracted revenue due over the next year for the fourth quarter, versus 21% growth excluding currency changes in the third quarter. For both businesses, recurring revenue is a more useful test of lasting demand than one quarter’s headline sales.
sections.heading: 1) Technology investors focus on future cash and revenue

sections.text:
Norwegian Cruise Line reported adjusted profit of $1.12 per share for its third quarter and raised its annual target to about $1.70. Stronger results improve the outlook, though the company still expects lower ticket-related revenue per passenger day in the fourth quarter.

Gen Digital’s second quarter of fiscal 2027 delivered revenue of $1.369 billion and adjusted profit of $0.74 per share. Its higher annual sales and profit ranges point to continued demand across cyber safety and financial-wellness products; retaining paying customers remains essential.

Carvana sold a record 217,385 vehicles in its third quarter, up 39%, and revenue grew 42% to $8.04 billion. It expects annual adjusted EBITDA near the high end of its earlier $2.7–$3.0 billion range. That profit measure excludes interest, taxes and several other costs, so cash generation and consumer financing conditions also matter.

Chipotle’s sales grew 9.6%, but restaurant margin fell to 23.3% from 24.5%. Its gain comes with a clear profitability question: can more visits and new restaurants offset rising operating costs?
sections.heading: 2) Better outlooks support cruise and consumer companies

sections.text:
Howmet’s third-quarter revenue rose 29% to $2.70 billion, supported by commercial aerospace and gas-turbine demand. It raised its annual outlook and set an initial 2027 revenue target of about $11.5 billion. Higher investment spending will make cash generation an important check on that growth.

Marvell is in advanced talks to buy Lumentum, according to reporting citing people familiar with the discussions. This remains a potential transaction. Data-center optics would expand Marvell’s AI infrastructure business, while financing and integration could affect shareholder returns.

title: October 30, 2026: Intel’s weak outlook hits technology shares as Mondelēz gains
summary: Intel’s warning about weak PC demand weighs on technology shares before open. Mondelēz benefits from improving volumes and margins, while Gilead raises its sales outlook.

sections.heading: 1) Technology outlooks drive the selloff
sections.text:
Intel’s October 29 earnings report paired strong recent data-center demand with a warning that the PC slowdown could persist into the first half of 2027. Its fourth-quarter revenue forecast is below third-quarter sales of $16.5 billion, shifting attention to the durability of demand.

Reddit’s October 29 warning concerned search traffic rather than a collapse in current advertising revenue: third-quarter sales grew 53%. Its planned tests of a more logged-in experience aim to strengthen direct engagement, but the audience risk remains.

Twilio’s fourth-quarter organic-growth forecast of 11%–12% compares with 16% in the third quarter. The slowdown matters because investors need sustained growth to support its valuation.

sections.heading: 2) Gainers show different routes to stronger profits
sections.text:
Mondelēz’s third-quarter volume and product mix improved 1.8%, while lower raw-material and manufacturing costs helped profitability. Its reaffirmed outlook makes continued margin recovery the key question.

Gilead raised its annual product-sales forecast from $30.1 billion–$30.4 billion to $31 billion–$31.3 billion. The stronger sales outlook should be distinguished from its wider expected annual loss, which includes acquisition-related research costs.

FedEx Freight’s first independent results cover June through September, a four-month transition period. Revenue rose 9.2% and adjusted operating profit rose 16.4%, while shipments declined 1.4%. Better pricing helps, but a volume recovery would provide a firmer foundation.

sections.heading: 4) What to watch next
sections.text:
The October 30 employment-cost report is scheduled before open. Wage and benefit costs matter for business margins and the inflation outlook.

Regeneron scheduled its third-quarter earnings release and conference call for October 30 before open. Dupixent growth and its eye-disease franchise are important questions for investors. Principal’s October 26 results provide recent context: operating profit per share rose to $2.22, while net investment outflows remained a risk.

Premarket prices can change sharply before regular trading begins. The next useful test is whether company outlooks support earnings expectations after these large price moves.
